name: Southeastern Monguor
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Dwyer, Arienne M. 2008. Tonogenesis in Southeastern Monguor. In K. David Harrison, David Rood & Arienne Dwyer (eds), Lessons from documented endangered languages (Typological Studies in Language 78), 111-128. Amsterdam: Benjamins. DOI 10.1075/tsl.78.05dwy. Author preprint, 33 pp., KU ScholarWorks hdl 1808/7055 (downloaded via the Internet Archive copy).
catalog_locator: Author preprint p. 7, sec. 2 'Contact environment and Mongolic prosody' (opening paragraph); p. 29, sec. 6 'Conclusions' (first paragraph); exceptions from sec. 2 (same paragraph), sec. 3.4 'Anomalous tonal patterns' and sec. 4 'Discussion' (paragraph after examples (17a-b)); morphology from sec. 4 and endnote 12
catalog_quote: The default prosodic pattern in SEM places lexical stress, which is realized by a raised tone melody, typically on the last syllable of the word. The raised tone melody is absent under two circumstances: in utterance-final syllables (where both downdrift and final prominence occur) and in final syllables of certain lexical pairs. Contrasting tone thus emerged in such latter examples, such as ‘cloth’ vs. ‘louse’ above, to avoid homophony. [...] This paper has identified two basic facts: (1) SEM has a default pitch rise on word boundaries. Since these tonal melodies are largely non-contrastive, these appear to be realizations of pitch accent or stress. Accent is placed on the last syllable of the word and is realized by a raised F0. (2) Additionally, the diachronic loss of segments (via for example syllable structure constraints) has sometimes led to homophony. Some of these words were native Mongolic, some entered SEM as loans. In order to distinguish potential cases of homophony, SEM assigned one of the pair a high tone, one low tone, making tone distinctive for a small set of items.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (prosodic accent) falls by default on the final syllable of the word; it is realized mainly by raised pitch (a rising/high F0 melody) rather than intensity, and it is not contrastive except in a small set of otherwise homophonous pairs where one member carries penultimate prominence with a final falling pitch (incipient pitch accent/tone).
new_statements.exceptions: (i) a handful of lexical pairs distinguished by prosody: bosi 'cloth' (final H) vs bosi 'louse' (penult + final falling), dasi 'we' vs dasi 'thread', chige 'ear' vs chige 'to see', wulang 'drinking' vs wulang 'many'; (ii) some inflectional suffixes (e.g. plural -si) do not attract stress, so prominence stays on the prior syllable; epenthetic vowels do not attract stress; (iii) utterance-final syllables show downdrift instead of the raised melody; (iv) Chinese loans take the same default final pattern regardless of original Chinese tone (unlike Baoan). Dwyer notes Slater 2003:103-104 treats both morphemes of some words as stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (lexical stress/boundary tone), based on elicited words in isolation and carrier utterances with F0 measurements from one main speaker (Wang Xianzhen, Minhe) plus later field checks; utterance-level intonation explicitly set aside.
new_statements.identity_note: Dwyer 2008 calls the variety 'Southeastern Monguor (SEM)', defined as the Monguor of Minhe county (Qinghai), i.e. Minhe Mangghuer = minh1238; her ISO code MJG covers Monguor as a whole (Huzhu Mongghul huzh1238 is her 'Northern Monguor'). Data are chiefly from one Minhe speaker (Wang Xianzhen) checked against other speakers.

sources.note: Default lexical stress, realized as a raised tone melody (raised F0), falls on the last syllable of the word; stress is not contrastive in Mongolic incl. SEM, but a small set of lexical pairs (bosi 'cloth' vs 'louse', dasi 'we' vs 'thread', chige 'ear' vs 'see', wulang 'drinking' vs 'many') now contrasts final H vs penult prominence + final falling pitch = incipient pitch accent/tone; suffixes that do not attract stress leave prominence on the penult; Chinese loans get the same default final pattern regardless of source tone (sec. 2 p. 7, sec. 4 pp. 22-27, conclusion p. 29).

tone.translation: Accent. In Tu (Minhe dialect), the accent falls on the final syllable of the word. [examples: 2-syllable shudú 'tooth', qará 'black', mɚɢá 'hat'; 3-syllable aŋʦɪdóŋ 'tasty', ʦuduorúo 'inside'; 4-syllable motúɢulú 'with wood', xaŋburawá 'let us rest']
